name: Angaataha
confidence_why: Le Moullec 2025, summarising his 2024 dissertation, puts stress on the first heaviest syllable with weight defined by vowel aperture and length and treats tone as a separate word-level property, while the earlier SIL descriptions (Lloyd 1973, R. Huisman 1980, R. Huisman 1992) tie stress to high tone and report lexically contrastive stress on low-tone words, so the weight-based reading rests on the fuller modern study but is known only from a short published summary against an older first-hand tradition that disagrees on the type of system.

catalog_quote: L’angaataha a six voyelles /i, e, a, aː, o, u/, avec une opposition de longueur entre les voyelles ouvertes /a/ et /aː/. ... La structure syllabique (C)(w)V(N) peut être régularisée, « réparée » (Hall, 2006: 407), en insérant un schwa non-phonémique ou une voyelle assimilée à son environnement: /pnpnipho/ [pə.nə.pə.ni.po.ˈho] « concombre ». L’accent d’intensité tombe sur la première syllabe la plus lourde; le poids est défini par l’aperture et la longueur des voyelles. Les mots sont aussi caractérisés par un ton de mot (word tone) H, L ou HL. Les propositions médiales ont une intonation montante et les propositions finales une intonation montante-descendante. [Le Moullec 2025, para. 4] || Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) There are three contrasting tones: high / ´ /, high-low / ˆ /, and low / ` /. naihɨrɨ 'knife' náihɨrɨ 'landslide' kîpɨ 'dirt' kipɨ̌ 'tree sp.' There are contrasting stress patterns on low tone words: 'otɨpɨho 'gourd' o'tɨpɨho 'bird sp.' [Huisman 1992 OPD p. 3] || Stress is predictable and occurs in conjunction with a high or a glide toneme. Any toneme occurs on any syllable of a word. [Lloyd 1973 p. 72]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Angaataha (anga1290) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Huisman & Lloyd 1981 'Angaatɨha tone, stress, and length' (LDAPS 12: 63-82), is on-topic but print-only: SIL archive entry 4100 has no digital file, the book (OCLC 8619473) is not in HathiTrust, Internet Archive or Google Books full view, and no search engine or repository copy exists — priority high for library acquisition. Through the SIL Language & Culture Archives listing for agm (the Internet Archive 2016) I found and obtained three further Angaataha documents (live SIL file host blocks all fetchers with an automated-access block; PDFs retrieved from Internet Archive copy): (1) Ronald Huisman's 1992 Organised Phonology Data, which states three contrasting tones and 'contrasting stress patterns on low tone words' ('otɨpɨho 'gourd' vs o'tɨpɨho 'bird sp.'); (2) Roberta Huisman's Dec. 1980 ms. on the prominence system (image scan, scanned, key page verified visually), which reports the target chapter's analysis: every syllable has a toneme and 'High and high-low incorporate stress and length'; (3) Eko & Graham 2014 grammar sketch, silent on word stress. Best first-hand statement: the 1992 OPD — Angaataha is a tone language in which stress is carried by high/high-low tone and is lexically contrastive on low-tone words, i.e. no fixed stress position.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Angaataha is a tone language (three tonemes in the 1980/1992 analyses: high, high-low, low; four in Lloyd 1973, adding a low-high glide), and stress is bound to tone: the high and high-low tonemes 'incorporate stress and length' (R. Huisman 1980, p. 1), i.e. stress falls on high-toned syllables, and 'Stress is predictable and occurs in conjunction with a high or a glide toneme. Any toneme occurs on any syllable of a word' (Lloyd 1973, p. 72) - so stress position is lexically determined via tone, not fixed by count. The 1992 OPD adds that on all-low-tone words stress itself is contrastive ('otɨpɨho 'gourd' vs o'tɨpɨho 'bird sp.'), so stress is not fully predictable from tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Contrastive stress on low-tone words (OPD 1992 p. 3) contradicts the earlier 'stress is predictable' summary (Lloyd 1973 p. 72). R. Huisman 1980 (pp. 1-2, 7ff.) describes discourse-conditioned tone on the last one or two suffixes of the word (high vs low on non-final suffix, high-low on final suffix) and total tone neutralization after question words; length is more pronounced on high-low tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (isolated words in the OPD). R. Huisman 1980 notes that inherent word tone except the last one or two syllables is retained in sentences, while the final suffix tones and stress-bearing high tones shift with discourse prominence; Lloyd 1973 p. 87 says tone-plus-stress 'usually occurs in connection with the grammatical stem'.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Angaataha = Angaatɨha = Angaatiha = Langimar [agm], Langimar Valley and Manki village, Aseki, Morobe Province; Lloyd 1973 p. 71: 'No dialect differences are known.' Glottolog anga1290 is the language-level code.

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the target chapter's first author: Angaataha is a three-toneme language (high, high-low, low; per R. Huisman 1980 p.1, citing the same chapter, every syllable bears a toneme and the high and high-low tonemes 'incorporate stress and length'). Word stress therefore has no fixed position: it rides on high/high-low tone, and on all-low-tone words its position is lexically contrastive (initial vs. second syllable in the 'gourd'/'bird sp.' pair). For a word-stress catalog this reads as: tone language, stress non-fixed / lexically contrastive (unpredictable), not weight- or edge-determined.

new_statements.translation: Intensity stress falls on the first heaviest syllable; weight is defined by the aperture and the length of the vowels. Words are also characterised by a word tone (word tone) H, L or HL. Medial clauses have a rising intonation and final clauses a rising-falling intonation.

Page meta: citation_authors 'Moullec, Yann Le', firstpage 245, lastpage 248, DC.language fr, publication date 2025/09/15. Reading weight-sensitive (leftmost heaviest syllable; weigh…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tone-language-with-stress reading (both have lexical tone plus a separate stress) but gives a new, explicit stress placement: weight-based (first heaviest syllable, weight = vowel aperture + length) rather than the 1973/1980/1992 SIL picture of stress riding on high tone or being lexically contrastive on low-tone words; it also re-analyses tone as word tone (H/L/HL) instead of syllable tone. It therefore changes the catalog's rule from 'lexically contrastive/unpredictable' to 'weight-sensitive', which is a contradiction in mechanism, though the type (tonal + stress) is the same.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress goes to the leftmost syllable of the highest weight in the word, where weight is a vowel-quality scale (more open vowels are heavier) combined with vowel length (/aː/ heavier than /a/); separately from stress, each word carries a word-level tone melody H, L or HL. The same paragraph's example /pnpnipho/ [pə.nə.pə.ni.po.ˈho] 'cucumber' shows final stress on the syllable with the full (non-epenthetic) open vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated (thesis summary; the full rule is in the 2024 INALCO thesis, which is not online: theses.fr s218049 accessible = non)
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe the same variety: Angaataha (Angaatɨha, Angaatiha, Langimar) of the Langimar valley, Menyamya district, Morobe Province, PNG (ISO agm). Le Moullec's fieldwork (2020, 2024) was in the same Langimar valley villages as the Huismans' SIL work of the 1970s-80s; no dialect split is mentioned in any source.

readall_conflicts: The sources disagree on the mechanism of stress, not on the presence of tone. The SIL-era descriptions held by the project (Lloyd 1973 p. 72 summarising Huisman & Huisman: 'Stress is predictable and occurs in conjunction with a high or a glide toneme'; R. Huisman 1980 p. 1: 'High and high-low incorporate stress and length'; R. Huisman OPD 1992 p. 3: 'contrasting stress patterns on low tone words: 'otɨpɨho gourd / o'tɨpɨho bird sp.') make stress a correlate of syllable tone, lexically contrastive only on all-low words; the newest first-hand analysis, Le Moullec 2025 (para 4, summarising the 2024 INALCO thesis), makes stress weight-sensitive ('first heaviest syllable', weight = vowel aperture + length) and independent of a word-level tone H/L/HL, i.e. it reanalyses syllable tone as word tone and stress as predictable from vowel weight. The 1981 Huisman & Lloyd chapter that the catalog and Glottolog cite for tone/stress/length is still not obtainable online, so the 1973/1980/1992 statements stand in for it second-hand. Le Moullec's example [pə.nə.pə.ni.po.ˈho] 'cucumber' (final stress on the only full open vowel) is consistent with his rule but cannot be checked against the OPD minimal pair without the thesis.

sources.citation: Huisman, Roberta D. 1980 [posted 2009]. The interplay of phonology and grammar in the Angaataha prominence system. 21 pp. ms. (draft), December 1980, SIL-PNG. SIL L&C Archives entry 31206.
sources.quote: There are three tonemes in Angaatɨha: high /´/, high low /ˆ/, and low /`/ which is not marked orthographically. Every syllable in a word has a toneme. High /´/ and /ˆ/ incorporate stress and length. Length is more pronounced on high low /ˆ/ tone (Huisman and Lloyd, 1980). Inherent word tone, except for the last one or two syllables of the word, is retained when words occur in sentences except in a question sentence.

sources.note: p. 1 sec. 2: 'There are three tonemes in Angaatɨha: high /´/, high low /ˆ/, and low /`/ which is not marked orthographically. Every syllable in a word has a toneme. High /´/ and /ˆ/ incorporate stress and length. Length is more pronounced on high low /ˆ/ tone (Huisman and Lloyd, 1980).' Rest of the paper is discourse: high vs low tone on the final/non-final suffix marks nuclear vs peripheral information; tone neutralized after question words.
